title: The Gurus' Muslim friends
hookLine: Mardana, Mian Mir, Budhu Shah, Nabi and Ghani Khan: the story is full of them

cards: Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan. Sher Muhammad Khan of Malerkotla. Rai Kalha of Raikot.
Say those names one after another, and something becomes hard to miss.

From the first Guru's travels to the tenth Guru's darkest winter, again and again at the turning points of the Sikh story, there's a Muslim friend standing close. Playing the music. Laying a foundation.

teach.b: Start at the beginning. Mardana, a Muslim musician from Guru Nanak's own village, traveled with him and played the rebab while the Guru sang.
Sikh tradition pictures Guru Nanak's hymns reaching people through the two of them together, the song and the strings. Then Mian Mir, the Sufi of Lahore and a friend of Guru Arjan.
Tradition credits Mian Mir with laying the foundation stone of the Harmandir.
Then Pir Budhu Shah, who sent his sons and followers to fight beside Guru Gobind Singh at Bhangani, where, tradition says, his sons fell.

Then the dark winter after Chamkaur: Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan carrying the Guru through enemy lines as a holy man, the Nawab of Malerkotla protesting the sentence on the Guru's youngest sons, and Rai Kalha sheltering the Guru and sending for news.
And there's a friendship older than any of them, inside the scripture itself.
The Guru Granth Sahib holds verses of Sheikh Farid, a Sufi poet, beside the hymns of the Gurus. The Sikh story has real enemies in it: an empire's cruelty, a governor's sentence.
But in the way Sikhs tell it, that cruelty never becomes a line drawn around a whole faith, because the friends keep turning up on the Guru's side of it. Look back at this week, too.
Todar Mal paid gold for the children's cremation. Rai Kalha gave shelter. Mai Bhago led the deserters back.
Bhai Mani Singh wrote steadily at Damdama. Bhai Jaita carried the head and was called a son. And the women of the Khalsa took a name that meant they belonged.

how: Sikhs remember Bhai Mardana, Mian Mir, Pir Budhu Shah, Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan, the Nawab of Malerkotla and Rai Kalha with gratitude, and Sheikh Farid's verses are read in the Guru Granth Sahib alongside the Gurus' hymns.

games.q: you're telling the Sikh story to a friend. the Gurus faced an empire's cruelty. how do you describe the Muslims in it?
o: as the enemy, all of them.
as people on every side, including close friends.
leave them out of the story.
games.why: the story itself won't draw a line around a whole faith: Mardana, Mian Mir, Budhu Shah, Nabi and Ghani Khan, Rai Kalha and more stood close.

practice: Bring to mind a friend who differs from you in some real way: another faith or none, another country, another generation.
Notice the difference plainly, without smoothing it over, then remember one specific time they stood close anyway. Quietly thank them, naming both the difference and the day.

wordCard.voice: Muslim friends. Mardana, Mian Mir, Budhu Shah, Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan, the Pathan brothers, the Nawab of Malerkotla, Rai Kalha, and Sheikh Farid inside the scripture itself. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: rebab, the stringed instrument Bhai Mardana played for Guru Nanak.

carryVoice: Your line: friends in every faith. At every turning point, someone stood close. That's the end of a week.
